topic: Property transactions and adjustments to income

notes.front: What is basis?
notes.back: The amount of your investment in property for tax purposes.
notes.explanation: Basis is used to figure depreciation, amortization, depletion, casualty losses, and gain or loss on a sale.
notes.example: Like the $12,000 you paid for shares: that figure is what a later sale price is measured against.
notes.source: Publication 551 (Rev. December 2025), Basis of Assets, “Introduction”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Basis is the amount of your investment in property for tax purposes. Use the basis of property to figure depreciation, amortization, depletion, and casualty losses.

notes.front: What is the cost basis of property you buy?
notes.back: Usually its cost, plus certain other costs you must capitalize (add to basis).
notes.explanation: Buying is the ordinary route into basis; gifts and inheritances follow other rules.
notes.example: Like a delivery van bought for $30,000: its cost basis starts at $30,000 before any adjustments.
notes.source: Publication 551 (Rev. December 2025), Basis of Assets, “Introduction”, p. 2
notes.evidence: The basis of property you buy is usually its cost. You may also have to capitalize (add to basis) certain other costs related to buying or producing the property.

notes.front: What is adjusted basis?
notes.back: Original basis after increases (such as improvements) and decreases (such as depreciation or casualty losses).
notes.explanation: Publication 551 says original basis is adjusted up or down by certain events, and the result is the adjusted basis.
notes.example: Like a $200,000 rental building with $30,000 of new roofing added and $25,000 of depreciation taken: its adjusted basis is $205,000.
notes.source: Publication 551 (Rev. December 2025), Basis of Assets, “Introduction”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Your original basis in property is adjusted (increased or decreased) by certain events. If you make improvements to the property, increase your basis. If you take deductions for depreciation or casualty losses, reduce your basis.

notes.front: What is the holding period of investment property, and how is it counted?
notes.back: How long you held it: counting starts the day after you acquired it and includes the day you disposed of it.
notes.explanation: The holding period decides whether gain or loss is long-term or short-term.
notes.example: Like shares bought on 10 March 2024 and sold on 10 March 2025: counting starts 11 March 2024, so they were held exactly 1 year, not more.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Long-term or Short-term”, p. 81
notes.evidence: To determine how long you held the investment property, begin counting on the date after the day you acquired the property. The day you disposed of the property is part of your holding period.

notes.front: What is depreciation recapture?
notes.back: Treating part of the gain on depreciated property as ordinary income because of depreciation taken on it.
notes.explanation: For section 1245 property, gain is ordinary income to the extent of depreciation allowed or allowable.
notes.example: Like selling a business machine for more than its depreciated value: the gain up to the depreciation taken is taxed as ordinary income.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Section 1245 Property”, p. 42
notes.evidence: A gain on the disposition of section 1245 property is treated as ordinary income to the extent of depreciation allowed or allowable on the property.

notes.front: What is section 1245 property?
notes.back: Property that is or has been depreciable or amortizable and is personal property, or certain other tangible property other than buildings.
notes.explanation: Personal property, tangible or intangible, is the first type Publication 544 lists.
notes.example: Like office computers, delivery vans or a patent being amortized.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Section 1245 property defined”, p. 42
notes.evidence: Section 1245 property includes any property that is or has been subject to an allowance for depreciation or amortization and that is any of the following types of property. 1. Personal property (either tangible or intangible).

notes.front: What is section 1250 property?
notes.back: Depreciable real property that is not and never has been section 1245 property.
notes.explanation: It includes a leasehold of land or of section 1250 property.
notes.example: Like a rented-out apartment building or a warehouse.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Section 1250 property defined”, p. 44
notes.evidence: This includes all real property that is subject to an allowance for depreciation and that is not and never has been section 1245 property.

notes.front: Which kinds of contract are section 1256 contracts? Give one example Publication 550 names.
notes.back: Contracts such as nonequity options: listed options that are not equity options, like broad-based stock index options.
notes.explanation: Nonequity options include debt options, commodity futures options, currency options and broad-based stock index options.
notes.example: Like an exchange-listed option on the S&P 500 index, rather than an option on one company's shares.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Section 1256 Contracts Marked to Market”, p. 56
notes.evidence: A section 1256 contract is any: Nonequity option. This is any listed option (defined later) that is not an equity option.

notes.front: What is a digital asset?
notes.back: Any digital representation of value recorded on a cryptographically secured distributed ledger or similar technology.
notes.explanation: The Form 1040 instructions name non-fungible tokens and virtual currencies such as cryptocurrencies and stablecoins.
notes.example: Like a bitcoin, a stablecoin, or a digital artwork token bought on a marketplace.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1040 and 1040-SR (2025), “Digital Assets”, p. 15
notes.evidence: Digital assets are any digital representations of value that are recorded on a cryptographically secured distributed ledger or any similar technology.

notes.front: What is Form 1099-DA?
notes.back: The form a broker should send you reporting a sale of a digital asset it handled for you.
notes.explanation: The Publication 17 reminder links it to sales effected through a broker.
notes.example: Like the year-end statement a crypto exchange sends listing your coin sales.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What's New: Form 1099-DA”, p. 3
notes.evidence: your broker should send you a Form 1099-DA that reports information regarding the transaction.

notes.front: How are passive activities held through a publicly traded partnership (PTP) treated?
notes.back: Separately: the passive rules are applied to each PTP on its own.
notes.explanation: Deductions from a PTP's passive activities can offset only income or gain from passive activities of the same PTP.
notes.example: Like units of a pipeline partnership bought on a stock exchange: its losses stay locked to that partnership's own income.
notes.source: Publication 925 (2025), Passive Activity and At-Risk Rules, “Publicly Traded Partnership”, p. 4
notes.evidence: You must apply the rules in this part separately to your income or loss from a passive activity held through a publicly traded partnership (PTP).

notes.front: What is an installment sale?
notes.back: A sale of property where you receive at least one payment after the tax year of the sale.
notes.explanation: The installment method lets you report part of the gain as each payment arrives.
notes.example: Like selling a plot of land in 2025 for five yearly payments starting in 2026.
notes.source: Publication 537 (2025), Installment Sales, “What's an Installment Sale?”, p. 1
notes.evidence: An installment sale is a sale of property where you receive at least one payment after the tax year of the sale.

notes.front: What is the gross profit percentage in an installment sale?
notes.back: Gross profit divided by contract price; that share of each payment (less interest) is installment sale income.
notes.explanation: The rest of each payment is a tax-free return of adjusted basis.
notes.example: Like a sale with $15,000 gross profit and a $60,000 contract price: 25% of each payment is taxable gain.
notes.source: Publication 537 (2025), Installment Sales, “Amount to report as installment sale income”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Multiply the payments you receive each year (less interest) by the gross profit percentage. The result is your installment sale income for the tax year.

notes.front: In installment sales to related persons, what is a second disposition?
notes.back: The related buyer disposing of the property before paying you in full, or within 2 years of the first sale.
notes.explanation: Then you may have to treat what the related person realizes as received by you.
notes.example: Like selling land to your son on a 10-year note, and your son selling it to a developer a year later.
notes.source: Publication 537 (2025), Installment Sales, “Sale and Later Disposition”, p. 10
notes.evidence: The related person makes the second disposition before making all payments on the first disposition. • The related person disposes of the property within 2 years of the first disposition.

notes.front: When does the alternate valuation date set the basis of inherited property?
notes.back: When the estate's personal representative chooses alternate valuation; basis is then the fair market value on that date.
notes.explanation: Otherwise basis is generally the fair market value at the date of death; Form 706 instructions explain the alternate date.
notes.example: Like an estate whose shares fall in value after the death, where the executor chooses the later valuation date for the estate tax return.
notes.source: Publication 551 (Rev. December 2025), Basis of Assets, “Inherited Property”, p. 15
notes.evidence: The FMV on the alternate valuation date if the personal representative for the estate chooses to use alternate valuation.

notes.front: What is a like-kind exchange?
notes.back: Exchanging business or investment real property solely for like-kind real property held for business or investment, recognizing no gain or loss.
notes.explanation: Publication 544 limits like-kind exchanges to real property held for use in a trade or business or for investment.
notes.example: Like swapping a rented-out duplex for a small office building you will also rent out.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Like-Kind Exchanges”, p. 16
notes.evidence: Generally, if you exchange real property you hold for use in a trade or business or hold for investment solely for other like-kind real property held for use in a trade or business or investment, you do not recognize the gain or loss

notes.front: What is a wash sale?
notes.back: Selling stock or securities at a loss and, within 30 days before or after, buying substantially identical stock or securities.
notes.explanation: Acquiring them in a fully taxable trade, among other acts, also counts.
notes.example: Like selling shares at a loss on 5 December and buying the same shares back on 20 December.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Wash Sales”, p. 86
notes.evidence: A wash sale occurs when you sell or trade stock or securities at a loss and within 30 days before or after the sale you: 1. Buy substantially identical stock or securities

notes.front: How is a nonbusiness bad debt deducted and reported?
notes.back: Only when totally worthless, as a short-term capital loss on Form 8949, Part I.
notes.explanation: A partly worthless nonbusiness debt can't be deducted.
notes.example: Like a personal loan to a former business partner who goes bankrupt and can never repay.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Nonbusiness Bad Debts”, p. 78
notes.evidence: deduct it as a nonbusiness bad debt in that year. Report it as a short-term capital loss on Form 8949, Part I, line 1

notes.front: For most taxpayers, what is modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) for the student loan interest deduction?
notes.back: Adjusted gross income figured before subtracting any student loan interest deduction.
notes.explanation: Each tax benefit defines its own MAGI; for student loan interest there may be other modifications.
notes.example: Like taking the adjusted gross income line of your return and adding back the student loan interest you subtracted.
notes.source: Publication 970 (2025), Tax Benefits for Education, “Modified adjusted gross income (MAGI)”, p. 34
notes.evidence: For most taxpayers, MAGI is AGI as figured on their federal income tax return before subtracting any deduction for student loan interest.

notes.front: What is self-employment tax (SE tax), and on which form is it figured?
notes.back: The tax on net earnings from self-employment, figured on Schedule SE (Form 1040).
notes.explanation: It applies at any age, even to people already getting social security or Medicare benefits.
notes.example: Like the social security and Medicare tax a freelance photographer pays on her own profit, since no employer withholds it.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule SE (Form 1040) (2025), “General Instructions”, p. 1
notes.evidence: Use Schedule SE (Form 1040) to figure the tax due on net earnings from self-employment.

notes.front: What is an elective deferral?
notes.back: Part of your compensation you choose to have your employer put into a retirement plan instead of paying it to you.
notes.explanation: The amount set aside is treated as an employer contribution to a qualified plan.
notes.example: Like having 6% of each pay cheque go into your 401(k) plan.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “Elective deferrals”, p. 53
notes.evidence: you can choose to have part of your compensation contributed by your employer to a retirement fund, rather than have it paid to you. The amount you set aside (called an elective deferral) is treated as an employer contribution to a qualified plan.

notes.front: What is a high deductible health plan (HDHP)?
notes.back: A health plan with a higher annual deductible than typical plans, and a maximum limit on out-of-pocket expenses.
notes.explanation: For 2025 the minimum deductible is $1,650 for self-only and $3,300 for family coverage.
notes.example: Like an insurance plan where you pay the first $2,000 of care each year yourself before the insurer pays.
notes.source: Publication 969 (2025), Health Savings Accounts and Other Tax-Favored Health Plans, “High deductible health plan (HDHP)”, p. 3
notes.evidence: An HDHP has: • A higher annual deductible than typical health plans, and

notes.front: What is a health savings account (HSA)?
notes.back: A tax-exempt trust or custodial account set up with a qualified trustee to pay or reimburse certain medical expenses.
notes.explanation: You must be an eligible individual to qualify for one.
notes.example: Like a bank account earmarked for doctor's bills, paired with a high-deductible insurance plan.
notes.source: Publication 969 (2025), Health Savings Accounts and Other Tax-Favored Health Plans, “Health Savings Accounts (HSAs)”, p. 3
notes.evidence: An HSA is a tax-exempt trust or custodial account you set up with a qualified HSA trustee to pay or reimburse certain medical expenses you incur.

notes.front: Who is an eligible individual for HSA contributions?
notes.back: Someone covered by an HDHP on the first day of the month, with no other health coverage, not in Medicare, and not a dependent.
notes.explanation: Other health coverage is allowed only where Publication 969 permits it.
notes.example: Like a 40-year-old on her employer's high-deductible plan with no other insurance, whom no one claims as a dependent.
notes.source: Publication 969 (2025), Health Savings Accounts and Other Tax-Favored Health Plans, “Qualifying for an HSA Contribution”, p. 3
notes.evidence: You are covered under a high deductible health plan (HDHP), described later, on the first day of the month. • You have no other health coverage except what is permitted under Other health coverage, later. • You aren't enrolled in Medicare.

notes.front: What is the HSA last-month rule?
notes.back: Being an eligible individual on the first day of the last month of your tax year (1 December for most) makes you eligible all year.
notes.explanation: Certain other requirements, including a testing period, also apply.
notes.example: Like someone who joins a high-deductible plan in November and is treated as eligible for the whole year.
notes.source: Publication 969 (2025), Health Savings Accounts and Other Tax-Favored Health Plans, “Last-month rule”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Under the last-month rule, you are considered to be an eligible individual for the entire year if you are an eligible individual on the first day of the last month of your tax year (December 1 for most taxpayers)

notes.front: What can an eligible educator deduct on Schedule 1, line 11 for 2025?
notes.back: Up to $300 of qualified expenses paid in 2025.
notes.explanation: If both spouses filing jointly were eligible educators, the maximum is $600.
notes.example: Like a fourth-grade teacher who buys $250 of classroom supplies with her own money.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1040 and 1040-SR (2025), “Schedule 1, line 11: Educator Expenses”, p. 93
notes.evidence: If you were an eligible educator in 2025, you can deduct on line 11 up to $300 of qualified expenses you paid in 2025.

notes.front: When should a lender send you Form 1099-A?
notes.back: When you abandon property securing a loan and the lender knows it has been abandoned.
notes.explanation: The form gives the information you need to figure your loss from the abandonment.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Forms 1099-A and 1099-C”, p. 7
notes.evidence: If you abandon property that secures a loan and the lender knows the property has been abandoned, the lender should send you Form 1099-A showing information you need to figure your loss from the abandonment.

notes.front: A lender cancels the debt on property a borrower abandoned and must file Form 1099-C. Will the borrower also get Form 1099-A?
notes.back: Not necessarily: the lender may put the abandonment information on Form 1099-C and send only that.
notes.explanation: Publication 544 allows the lender to combine both on Form 1099-C.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Forms 1099-A and 1099-C”, p. 7
notes.evidence: the lender may include the information about the abandonment on that form instead of on Form 1099-A and send you Form 1099-C only.

notes.front: On a sale of section 1245 property, how is gain above the depreciation recapture treated?
notes.back: As section 1231 gain.
notes.explanation: Only the part up to depreciation is ordinary income.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Section 1245 Property”, p. 42
notes.evidence: Any gain recognized that is more than the part that is ordinary income from depreciation is a section 1231 gain.

notes.front: A contractor sells equipment for $50,000. It cost $60,000 and $25,000 of depreciation was taken. How much gain is ordinary income?
notes.back: All $15,000 of gain.
notes.explanation: Adjusted basis: $60,000 − $25,000 = $35,000. Gain: $50,000 − $35,000 = $15,000. Depreciation of $25,000 exceeds the gain, so the whole $15,000 is recaptured.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Section 1245 Property”, p. 42
notes.evidence: A gain on the disposition of section 1245 property is treated as ordinary income to the extent of depreciation allowed or allowable on the property.

notes.front: For section 1250 property, how much gain is ordinary income?
notes.back: Gain up to the additional depreciation allowed or allowable.
notes.explanation: Only additional depreciation is recaptured, not all depreciation as for section 1245 property.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Section 1250 Property”, p. 44
notes.evidence: Gain on the disposition of section 1250 property is treated as ordinary income to the extent of additional depreciation allowed or allowable on the property.

notes.front: For section 1250 property held longer than 1 year, what is additional depreciation?
notes.back: Actual depreciation adjustments that are more than depreciation figured with the straight-line method.
notes.explanation: So a building depreciated only by straight line has no additional depreciation.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Additional Depreciation”, p. 44
notes.evidence: If you hold section 1250 property longer than 1 year, the additional depreciation is the actual depreciation adjustments that are more than the depreciation figured using the straight-line method.

notes.front: Which is section 1245 property and which section 1250: a depreciated delivery truck, and a depreciated warehouse?
notes.back: The truck is section 1245 property; the warehouse is section 1250 property.
notes.explanation: Personal property falls under section 1245; depreciable real property never under section 1245 is section 1250 property.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Section 1250 property defined”, p. 44
notes.evidence: This includes all real property that is subject to an allowance for depreciation and that is not and never has been section 1245 property.

notes.front: When is a gain on investment property long-term?
notes.back: When you held the property more than 1 year; 1 year or less is short-term.
notes.explanation: The holding period is counted from the day after acquisition.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Long-term or Short-term”, p. 81
notes.evidence: If you hold investment property more than 1 year, any capital gain or loss is a long-term capital gain or loss. If you hold the property 1 year or less, any capital gain or loss is a short-term capital gain or loss.

notes.front: Kai bought shares on 3 February 2024 and sold them at a gain on 3 February 2025. Short-term or long-term?
notes.back: Short-term.
notes.explanation: Counting starts 4 February 2024 and includes 3 February 2025: exactly 1 year, not more than 1 year.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Long-term or Short-term”, p. 81
notes.evidence: To determine how long you held the investment property, begin counting on the date after the day you acquired the property.

notes.front: What is net capital gain?
notes.back: The amount by which net long-term capital gain is more than net short-term capital loss.
notes.explanation: This is the amount that can qualify for the lower capital gain rates.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Capital Gain Tax Rates”, p. 103
notes.evidence: The term "net capital gain" means the amount by which your net long-term capital gain for the year is more than your net short-term capital loss.

notes.front: What are the maximum capital gain rates for 2025?
notes.explanation: The 28% rate applies to items such as collectibles gain.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Capital Gain Tax Rates”, p. 103
notes.evidence: For 2025, the maximum capital gain rates are 0%, 15%, 20%, 25%, and 28%.

notes.front: In 2025 Ash has $6,000 long-term gain, $2,000 long-term loss and $1,500 short-term loss. What is the net capital gain?
notes.explanation: Net the long-term items first ($6,000 − $2,000 = $4,000), then subtract the net short-term loss of $1,500 from that.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Capital Gain Tax Rates”, p. 103
notes.evidence: The term "net capital gain" means the amount by which your net long-term capital gain for the year is more than your net short-term capital loss.

notes.front: What is the most net capital loss you can deduct against other income in a year?
notes.back: $3,000, or $1,500 if married filing separately, or your total net loss if smaller.
notes.explanation: The allowable deduction is figured on Schedule D.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Capital Losses: Limit on deduction”, p. 101
notes.evidence: Your allowable capital loss deduction, figured on Schedule D (Form 1040), is the lesser of: • $3,000 ($1,500 if you are married and file a separate return), or

notes.front: What happens to a net capital loss above the yearly limit?
notes.back: It carries over to the next year and later years until used up, treated as incurred in that next year.
notes.explanation: There is no end date for the carryover in Publication 550's rule.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Capital Loss Carryover”, p. 102
notes.evidence: you can carry over the unused part to the next year and treat it as if you had incurred it in that next year. If part of the loss is still unused, you can carry it over to later years until it is completely used up.

notes.front: Single filer Bea has a $10,000 net capital loss in 2025. How much is deductible in 2025, and how much carries over?
notes.back: $3,000 deducted; $7,000 carried over.
notes.explanation: The limit is the lesser of $3,000 and $10,000. $10,000 − $3,000 = $7,000 carries to 2026.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Capital Losses: Limit on deduction”, p. 101
notes.evidence: Your allowable capital loss deduction, figured on Schedule D (Form 1040), is the lesser of: • $3,000 ($1,500 if you are married and file a separate return), or

notes.front: What happens to a section 1256 contract still held at year end?
notes.back: It is generally treated as sold at fair market value on the last business day of the year, and gain or loss is recognized.
notes.explanation: This is the mark-to-market rule; hedging transactions are excepted.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Mark-to-Market Rule”, p. 57
notes.evidence: A section 1256 contract that you hold at the end of the tax year will generally be treated as sold at its fair market value on the last business day of the tax year, and you must recognize any gain or loss that results.

notes.front: A trader's section 1256 contracts show a $10,000 gain for 2025, all held under 2 months. How is it split?
notes.back: $6,000 long-term and $4,000 short-term capital gain.
notes.explanation: Under the 60/40 rule, 60% × $10,000 = $6,000 long-term and 40% × $10,000 = $4,000 short-term, whatever the holding period.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “60/40 rule”, p. 57
notes.evidence: 60% of your capital gain or loss will be treated as a long-term capital gain or loss, and 40% will be treated as a short-term capital gain or loss. This is true regardless of how long you actually held the property.

notes.front: If you receive Form 1099-DA, must you still answer the digital asset question on Form 1040?
notes.back: Yes. The question on page 1 must be answered whether or not you received Form 1099-DA.
notes.explanation: You must also report gain or loss from the digital asset transactions.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1040 and 1040-SR (2025), “What's New: Form 1099-DA”, p. 6
notes.evidence: you must answer the digital asset question on Form 1040 whether or not you received a Form 1099-DA, and you must report gain or loss from the transaction with respect to the digital assets

notes.front: In 2025 Zoe sold stablecoins through a broker at a small gain. What must Zoe do on Form 1040?
notes.back: Answer the digital asset question and report the gain.
notes.explanation: Stablecoins are digital assets, and a sale must be reported whether or not a Form 1099-DA arrives.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1040 and 1040-SR (2025), “Digital Assets”, p. 15
notes.evidence: For example, digital assets include non-fungible tokens (NFTs) and virtual currencies, such as cryptocurrencies and stablecoins.

notes.front: A 2025 Form 1099-DA shows proceeds but a blank basis box. Is the broker in breach, and does the sale still get reported?
notes.back: No breach: basis reporting is optional for 2025. The sale is still reported, using your own basis records.
notes.explanation: The broker should send Form 1099-DA for the sale, but basis reporting was optional in 2025.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What's New: Form 1099-DA”, p. 3
notes.evidence: your broker should send you a Form 1099-DA that reports information regarding the transaction. In 2025, your broker has the option to report your basis in the digital asset on Form 1099-DA but is not required to do so.

notes.front: When you receive more shares in a nontaxable stock dividend or stock split, what happens to your original shares' basis?
notes.back: You must reduce it: the same total basis is spread over more shares.
notes.explanation: Publication 550 requires the basis of the original stock to be reduced.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Adjusted Basis”, p. 62
notes.evidence: if you receive more stock from nontaxable stock dividends or stock splits, you must reduce the basis of your original stock.

notes.front: Eli owns 100 shares with a $3,000 basis. A 2-for-1 stock split gives him 200 shares. What is his basis per share?
notes.explanation: Total basis stays $3,000, spread over 200 shares: $3,000 ÷ 200 = $15, down from $30.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Adjusted Basis”, p. 62
notes.evidence: if you receive more stock from nontaxable stock dividends or stock splits, you must reduce the basis of your original stock.

notes.front: Which improvements increase the basis of property?
notes.back: Items properly added to a capital account, including improvements with a useful life of more than 1 year.
notes.explanation: Such additions are capitalized, not deducted.
notes.source: Publication 551 (Rev. December 2025), Basis of Assets, “Increases to Basis”, p. 6
notes.evidence: Increase the basis of any property by all items properly added to a capital account. These include the cost of any improvements having a useful life of more than 1 year.

notes.front: A buyer pays $1,200 of real estate taxes the seller owed, and the seller doesn't reimburse her. How are they treated?
notes.back: Added to the buyer's basis in the property, not deducted as taxes.
notes.explanation: Taxes the seller owed and the buyer paid without reimbursement become part of basis.
notes.source: Publication 551 (Rev. December 2025), Basis of Assets, “Real estate taxes”, p. 3
notes.evidence: If you pay real estate taxes the seller owed on real property you bought, and the seller didn't reimburse you, treat those taxes as part of your basis. You can't deduct them as taxes.

notes.front: If the fair market value of gifted property is at least the donor's adjusted basis, what is your basis?
notes.back: The donor's adjusted basis when you received the gift, increased by all or part of any gift tax paid.
notes.explanation: The donor's basis carries over to you.
notes.source: Publication 551 (Rev. December 2025), Basis of Assets, “FMV Equal to or More Than Donor's Adjusted Basis”, p. 14
notes.evidence: If the FMV of the property is equal to or greater than the donor's adjusted basis, your basis is the donor's adjusted basis at the time you received the gift.

notes.front: A parent gives shares with a $4,000 adjusted basis, worth $9,000, to a child, who later sells them for $10,000. No gift tax was paid. What is the child's gain?
notes.explanation: Value at the gift ($9,000) exceeds the donor's basis, so the child takes the $4,000 basis: $10,000 − $4,000 = $6,000.
notes.source: Publication 551 (Rev. December 2025), Basis of Assets, “FMV Equal to or More Than Donor's Adjusted Basis”, p. 14
notes.evidence: If the FMV of the property is equal to or greater than the donor's adjusted basis, your basis is the donor's adjusted basis at the time you received the gift.

notes.front: If gifted property's fair market value at the gift was below the donor's adjusted basis, what bases apply?
notes.back: For gain, the donor's adjusted basis; for loss, the fair market value when you received the gift (each adjusted while you held it).
notes.explanation: Your basis depends on whether you have a gain or a loss when you dispose of it.
notes.source: Publication 551 (Rev. December 2025), Basis of Assets, “FMV Less Than Donor's Adjusted Basis”, p. 14
notes.evidence: Your basis for figuring gain is the same as the donor's adjusted basis plus or minus any required adjustment to basis while you held the property. Your basis for figuring loss is its FMV when you received the gift

notes.front: Shares with a donor basis of $10,000 were worth $7,000 when gifted. The recipient sells for $6,000. What is the loss?
notes.explanation: Value at the gift was below donor basis, and the sale is at a loss, so loss basis is $7,000: $6,000 − $7,000 = −$1,000.
notes.source: Publication 551 (Rev. December 2025), Basis of Assets, “FMV Less Than Donor's Adjusted Basis”, p. 14
notes.evidence: Your basis for figuring loss is its FMV when you received the gift plus or minus any required adjustment to basis while you held

notes.front: Same gift (donor basis $10,000, worth $7,000 when given), but the recipient sells for $12,000. What is the gain?
notes.explanation: A sale at a gain uses the donor's $10,000 basis: $12,000 − $10,000 = $2,000.
notes.source: Publication 551 (Rev. December 2025), Basis of Assets, “FMV Less Than Donor's Adjusted Basis”, p. 14
notes.evidence: Your basis for figuring gain is the same as the donor's adjusted basis plus or minus any required adjustment to basis while you held the property.

notes.front: Generally, what sets your basis in property you inherit from a decedent?
notes.back: Its fair market value at the date of death, or on the alternate valuation date if the personal representative chooses it.
notes.explanation: Special-use valuation and some other cases can give different figures.
notes.source: Publication 551 (Rev. December 2025), Basis of Assets, “Inherited Property”, p. 15
notes.evidence: Generally, the basis of property inherited from a decedent is one of the following. 1. The FMV of the property at the date of the individual's death.

notes.front: Rin inherits a house her father bought for $90,000. It was worth $310,000 at his death; no alternate valuation was chosen. She sells it for $320,000. What is her gain?
notes.back: $10,000, before selling costs.
notes.explanation: Basis is value at death, $310,000, not the father's cost: $320,000 − $310,000 = $10,000.
notes.source: Publication 551 (Rev. December 2025), Basis of Assets, “Inherited Property”, p. 15
notes.evidence: The FMV of the property at the date of the individual's death.

notes.front: Shares cost the owner $5,000 and are worth $20,000. What basis would a recipient take if they were given as a gift, and if they were inherited at that value?
notes.back: Gift: $5,000 (the donor's basis). Inherited: $20,000 (value at death).
notes.explanation: A gift worth more than the donor's basis carries that basis over; inheritance generally uses fair market value at death.
notes.source: Publication 551 (Rev. December 2025), Basis of Assets, “Inherited Property”, p. 15
notes.evidence: Generally, the basis of property inherited from a decedent is one of the following.

notes.front: Ivy has a $3,000 passive loss from PTP A and $5,000 of passive income from PTP B. Can the loss offset the income?
notes.back: No. PTP A's loss can offset only passive income from PTP A.
notes.explanation: Each PTP is treated separately, so the $3,000 is carried forward within PTP A.
notes.source: Publication 925 (2025), Passive Activity and At-Risk Rules, “Publicly Traded Partnership”, p. 4
notes.evidence: You can offset deductions from passive activities of a PTP only against income or gain from passive activities of the same PTP.

notes.front: How much gain from selling a main home can be excluded under section 121?
notes.back: Up to $250,000, or $500,000 for a married couple filing jointly.
notes.explanation: The full exclusion requires meeting the Eligibility Test.
notes.source: Publication 523 (2025), Selling Your Home, “Introduction”, p. 2
notes.evidence: you may exclude the first $250,000 of gain from the sale of your home from your income and avoid paying taxes on it. The exclusion is increased to $500,000 for a married couple filing jointly.

notes.front: What is the residence requirement for the home sale exclusion?
notes.back: Owning and using the home as your residence for at least 24 months of the previous 5 years.
notes.explanation: The 24 months need not be one block; a total of 24 months (730 days) is enough.
notes.source: Publication 523 (2025), Selling Your Home, “Eligibility Step 3—Residence”, p. 3
notes.evidence: If you owned the home and used it as your residence for at least 24 months of the previous 5 years, you meet the residence requirement. The 24 months of residence can fall anywhere within the 5-year period

notes.front: Single filer Lin sells the home she owned and lived in for 6 years at a $290,000 gain. How much is taxable?
notes.explanation: She meets the ownership and residence tests. $290,000 − $250,000 exclusion = $40,000 taxable.
notes.source: Publication 523 (2025), Selling Your Home, “Introduction”, p. 2
notes.evidence: you may exclude the first $250,000 of gain from the sale of your home from your income and avoid paying taxes on it.

notes.front: A married couple filing jointly, both meeting the tests, sell their main home at a $430,000 gain. How much is taxable?
notes.back: None: the gain is within the $500,000 exclusion.
notes.explanation: $430,000 is less than $500,000, so the whole gain is excluded.
notes.source: Publication 523 (2025), Selling Your Home, “Introduction”, p. 2
notes.evidence: The exclusion is increased to $500,000 for a married couple filing jointly.

notes.front: Tom lived in his home 2020–2021, rented it out 2022–2023, and moved back in January 2024 until selling in March 2025. Does he meet the residence requirement?
notes.back: Yes. His residence adds up to at least 24 months within the previous 5 years.
notes.explanation: Only the 5 years before the March 2025 sale count, from March 2020: about 22 months in 2020–2021 plus about 14 from January 2024, well over 24. The months need not be continuous.
notes.source: Publication 523 (2025), Selling Your Home, “Eligibility Step 3—Residence”, p. 3
notes.evidence: The 24 months of residence can fall anywhere within the 5-year period, and it doesn't have to be a single block of time.

notes.front: Within how long after a spouse's death can an unmarried surviving spouse sell the home and still use the $500,000 exclusion?
notes.back: Within 2 years of the death, if the other conditions are met.
notes.explanation: The survivor must not have remarried, among other conditions.
notes.source: Publication 523 (2025), Selling Your Home, “Surviving spouse”, p. 4
notes.evidence: You sell your home within 2 years of the death of your spouse. 2. You haven't remarried at the time of the sale.

notes.front: When both section 121 and section 1031 apply to a home converted to a rental and exchanged, which applies first?
notes.back: Section 121 is applied first to realized gain; section 1031 then applies.
notes.explanation: Publication 523 sets this order when both sets of requirements are met.
notes.source: Publication 523 (2025), Selling Your Home, “Exchange of home”, p. 6
notes.evidence: If the requirements of both sections 1031 and 121 are met, the section 121 exclusion is applied first to realized gain; section 1031 then applies

notes.front: Can you use the installment method to report a loss?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: The installment method applies only to gains.
notes.source: Publication 537 (2025), Installment Sales, “Introduction”, p. 1
notes.evidence: You can't use the installment method to report a loss.

notes.front: A furniture shop sells a sofa from inventory to a customer paying in instalments over 2 years. Is it an installment sale?
notes.back: No. The regular sale of inventory doesn't qualify even with later payments.
notes.explanation: Publication 537 excludes regular inventory sales from the installment method.
notes.source: Publication 537 (2025), Installment Sales, “What's an Installment Sale?”, p. 2
notes.evidence: The regular sale of inventory of personal property doesn't qualify as an installment sale even if you receive a payment after the year of sale.

notes.front: In an installment sale, how is gross profit figured?
notes.back: Selling price minus your adjusted basis for installment sale purposes.
notes.explanation: For a home, excludable gain is also subtracted.
notes.source: Publication 537 (2025), Installment Sales, “Gross profit”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Gross profit is the total gain you report on the installment method. To figure your gross profit, subtract your adjusted basis for installment sale purposes from the selling price.

notes.front: Jess sells land with a $30,000 adjusted basis for $80,000, receiving $20,000 in 2025 and the rest later (ignore interest). How much gain does Jess report for 2025?
notes.source: Publication 537 (2025), Installment Sales, “Amount to report as installment sale income”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Multiply the payments you receive each year (less interest) by the gross profit percentage. The result is your installment sale income for the tax year.

notes.front: In an installment sale of depreciated property, when is depreciation recapture reported?
notes.back: All in the year of sale, whether or not a payment is received that year.
notes.explanation: It is figured on Form 4797 and reported as ordinary income in the year of sale.
notes.source: Publication 537 (2025), Installment Sales, “Depreciation Recapture Income”, p. 9
notes.evidence: you must report any depreciation recapture income in the year of sale, whether or not an installment payment was received that year.

notes.front: In December 2025 Omar sells equipment on a note paid in 2026–2030. $18,000 of the gain is section 1245 recapture. When is the $18,000 taxed?
notes.back: In 2025, the year of sale, even though no payment was received that year.
notes.explanation: Recapture income is reported in full in the year of sale; only gain beyond it is spread over the payments.
notes.source: Publication 537 (2025), Installment Sales, “Depreciation Recapture Income”, p. 9
notes.evidence: you must report any depreciation recapture income in the year of sale, whether or not an installment payment was received that year.

notes.front: If you sell depreciable property to certain related persons, can you generally use the installment method?
notes.back: Generally no; all payments to be received are treated as received in the year of sale.
notes.explanation: Publication 537 notes an exception to this rule.
notes.source: Publication 537 (2025), Installment Sales, “Sale of Depreciable Property”, p. 9
notes.evidence: sell depreciable property to certain related persons, you generally can't report the sale using the installment method. Instead, all payments to be received are considered received in the year of sale.

notes.front: A business owner sells a depreciable delivery van to her controlled company on a 3-year note. Assuming no exception, when is the gain reported?
notes.back: All in the year of sale.
notes.explanation: For depreciable property sold to certain related persons, all payments are treated as received in the year of sale.
notes.source: Publication 537 (2025), Installment Sales, “Sale of Depreciable Property”, p. 9
notes.evidence: Instead, all payments to be received are considered received in the year of sale.

notes.front: After a related buyer's second disposition, what may the original seller have to do?
notes.back: Treat the amount the related person realizes as received by the seller when the related person disposes of it.
notes.explanation: This can accelerate gain the seller was deferring.
notes.source: Publication 537 (2025), Installment Sales, “Sale to a related person”, p. 9
notes.evidence: you may have to treat the amount realized by the related person as received by you when the related person disposes of the property.

notes.front: In 2024 Ada sold land to her daughter on a 10-year installment note. In 2025 the daughter sells the land for cash. What must Ada consider?
notes.back: The second disposition rule: Ada may have to treat what her daughter realized as received by Ada in 2025.
notes.explanation: The daughter disposed of the land within 2 years and before paying in full.
notes.source: Publication 537 (2025), Installment Sales, “Sale and Later Disposition”, p. 10
notes.evidence: The related person disposes of the property within 2 years of the first disposition.

notes.front: A seller sells marketable securities to a sibling on instalments; the sibling resells within 2 years. Does the 2-year second disposition rule apply?
notes.back: No. The 2-year rule doesn't apply to marketable securities.
notes.explanation: Publication 537 carves marketable securities out of that part of the rule.
notes.source: Publication 537 (2025), Installment Sales, “Sale and Later Disposition”, p. 10
notes.evidence: This rule doesn't apply if the property involved is marketable securities.

notes.front: Who can tell you whether your stock option is statutory or nonstatutory?
notes.back: Your employer.
notes.explanation: The kind of option decides whether you have income at grant, at exercise or only at sale.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Stock Options”, p. 11
notes.evidence: Your employer can tell you which kind of option you hold.

notes.front: Two employees each receive options: one gets ISOs, the other nonstatutory options that trade on an exchange. Who may have income at grant?
notes.back: The nonstatutory option holder; ISOs create no income at grant or exercise.
notes.explanation: An actively traded option has a readily determinable value, so the nonstatutory option can be taxed at grant.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Nonstatutory Stock Options”, p. 11
notes.evidence: The FMV of an option can be readily determined if it's actively traded on an established market.

notes.front: In a deferred like-kind exchange, within how many days must you identify the replacement property?
notes.back: 45 days after transferring the property given up.
notes.explanation: This is called the identification period.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Deferred Exchanges: identification requirement”, p. 18
notes.evidence: the property to be received within 45 days after the date you transfer the property given up in the exchange. This period of time is called the identification period.

notes.front: In a like-kind exchange at a gain, what if you also receive money or other property?
notes.back: You recognize gain up to the money plus the fair market value of the non-like-kind property received.
notes.explanation: The exchange is then partly nontaxable.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Partially Nontaxable Exchanges”, p. 23
notes.evidence: you must recognize the gain you realize (see Amount recognized, earlier) to the extent of the money and the FMV of the non-like-kind property you receive in the exchange.

notes.front: Ben exchanges investment land (basis $100,000) for a rental lot worth $150,000 plus $20,000 cash. What gain is recognized?
notes.explanation: Realized gain: $170,000 − $100,000 = $70,000. Recognized only up to the $20,000 cash; $50,000 is deferred.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Partially Nontaxable Exchanges”, p. 23
notes.evidence: you must recognize the gain you realize (see Amount recognized, earlier) to the extent of the money and the FMV of the non-like-kind property you receive in the exchange.

notes.front: A landscaper trades an old business truck for a newer one. Is it a like-kind exchange?
notes.back: No. Like-kind exchanges apply only to real property held for business or investment.
notes.explanation: Publication 544 limits nonrecognition to exchanges of real property.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Like-Kind Exchanges”, p. 49
notes.evidence: The nonrecognition rules for like-kind exchanges only apply to exchanges of real property held for investment or for productive use in your trade or business.

notes.front: Can depreciation recapture arise in a like-kind exchange even if no gain would otherwise be recognized?
notes.back: Yes. Section 1245 recapture may occur when non-section 1245 property is received in the exchange.
notes.explanation: Publication 544 gives this as an exception to nonrecognition.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Like-kind exchanges and involuntary conversions”, p. 49
notes.evidence: section 1245 recapture may occur when property that is not section 1245 property is received as part of a like-kind exchange or involuntary conversion even if no gain would otherwise be recognized.

notes.front: Nia lent a friend $5,000; the friend has repaid $1,000 and may repay some more. Can Nia deduct the remaining $4,000 now?
notes.back: No. A partly worthless nonbusiness debt can't be deducted.
notes.explanation: The debt must be totally worthless before any nonbusiness bad debt deduction.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Deductible nonbusiness bad debts”, p. 83
notes.evidence: To be deductible, nonbusiness bad debts must be totally worthless. You cannot deduct a partly worthless nonbusiness debt.

notes.front: Pat gave a relative $8,000 with no note and no expectation of repayment. Later Pat claims a bad debt. What must Pat show?
notes.back: That at the time there was an intention to make a loan and not a gift.
notes.explanation: Without that intention the transfer is a gift, not a deductible bad debt.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Loan or gift”, p. 83
notes.evidence: For a bad debt, you must show there was an intention at the time of the transaction to make a loan and not a gift.

notes.front: A $6,000 personal loan made in 2023 becomes totally worthless in 2025. How is it reported?
notes.back: As a $6,000 short-term capital loss for 2025 on Form 8949, Part I.
notes.explanation: Nonbusiness bad debts are short-term capital losses regardless of how long the loan was outstanding.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Nonbusiness Bad Debts”, p. 78
notes.evidence: Report it as a short-term capital loss on Form 8949, Part I, line 1

notes.front: What happens to a loss disallowed by the wash sale rules?
notes.back: It is added to the cost of the new stock or securities, giving their basis.
notes.explanation: The adjustment postpones the loss until you dispose of the new shares.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Wash Sales”, p. 86
notes.evidence: If your loss was disallowed because of the wash sale rules, add the disallowed loss to the cost of the new stock or securities (except in (4) above). The result is your basis in the new stock or securities.

notes.front: Uma buys 50 shares for $2,000, sells them for $1,400 on 10 November, and buys 50 of the same shares for $1,500 on 25 November. What is her loss and new basis?
notes.back: The $600 loss is disallowed; her new basis is $2,100.
notes.explanation: Repurchase within 30 days makes a wash sale. Loss: $2,000 − $1,400 = $600, added to the $1,500 cost: $2,100.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Wash Sales”, p. 86
notes.evidence: If your loss was disallowed because of the wash sale rules, add the disallowed loss to the cost of the new stock or securities

notes.front: Vic buys more shares of a stock on 1 December, then sells older shares of it at a loss on 20 December. Can this be a wash sale?
notes.back: Yes. The window runs 30 days before as well as after the sale.
notes.explanation: 1 December is 19 days before the sale, inside the 30-day window.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Wash Sales”, p. 86
notes.evidence: within 30 days before or after the sale you: 1. Buy substantially identical stock or securities

notes.front: Wes sells shares at a loss on 1 March and buys the same shares back on 1 April (31 days later). Wash sale?
notes.back: No. The repurchase falls outside the 30-day window.
notes.explanation: Only purchases within 30 days before or after the sale count.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Wash Sales”, p. 86
notes.evidence: A wash sale occurs when you sell or trade stock or securities at a loss and within 30 days before or after the sale you

notes.front: Hal sells stock with a $9,000 basis to his brother for $6,000; the brother later sells it to a stranger for $10,000. What gain does the brother report?
notes.explanation: Hal's $3,000 loss is disallowed. The brother's gain is $10,000 − $6,000 = $4,000, reduced by the $3,000: $1,000.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Related Party Transactions”, p. 74
notes.evidence: If you sell or trade at a loss property you acquired from a related party, you cannot recognize the loss that was not allowed to the related party.

notes.front: To be in business as a trader in securities, what must you seek to profit from?
notes.back: Daily market movements in prices, not dividends, interest or capital appreciation.
notes.explanation: This is one of the conditions that must all be met.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Special Rules for Traders in Securities or Commodities”, p. 104
notes.evidence: You must seek to profit from daily market movements in the prices of securities or commodities and not from dividends, interest, or capi

notes.front: Fay buys dividend stocks and holds them for years, checking prices monthly. Is she a trader in securities?
notes.back: No. She seeks dividends and appreciation, not daily price movements, so she is an investor.
notes.explanation: A trader must seek profit from daily market movements.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Special Rules for Traders in Securities or Commodities”, p. 104
notes.evidence: To be engaged in business as a trader in securities or commodities, you must meet all the following conditions.

notes.front: At what level of net earnings from self-employment must you pay SE tax?
notes.back: $400 or more.
notes.explanation: A lower threshold ($108.28) applies to church employee income.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule SE (Form 1040) (2025), “Who Must Pay SE Tax”, p. 1
notes.evidence: pay SE tax if you had net earnings of $400 or more as a self-employed person.

notes.front: A student earns a $380 net profit from weekend dog walking and has no other self-employment income. Does SE tax apply?
notes.back: No. Net earnings are under $400.
notes.explanation: $380 is less than the $400 threshold.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule SE (Form 1040) (2025), “Who Must Pay SE Tax”, p. 1
notes.evidence: pay SE tax if you had net earnings of $400 or more as a self-employed person.

notes.front: Does SE tax stop once you are old enough to receive social security?
notes.back: No. It applies at any age, even if you already get social security or Medicare benefits.
notes.explanation: The Schedule SE instructions say the tax applies no matter how old you are.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule SE (Form 1040) (2025), “General Instructions”, p. 1
notes.evidence: This tax applies no matter how old you are and even if you are already getting social security or Medicare benefi

notes.front: For 2025, the maximum self-employment income subject to social security tax is {{c1::$176,100}}.
notes.explanation: Above this amount, only the Medicare part of SE tax continues.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule SE (Form 1040) (2025), “What's New”, p. 1
notes.evidence: For 2025, the maximum amount of self-employment income subject to social security tax is $176,100.

notes.front: A consultant has $200,000 of self-employment income subject to SE tax and no wages. On how much does the social security part apply?
notes.explanation: Social security tax stops at the $176,100 maximum; the $23,900 above it is not subject to that part.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule SE (Form 1040) (2025), “What's New”, p. 1
notes.evidence: For 2025, the maximum amount of self-employment income subject to social security tax is $176,100.

notes.front: Where is the deductible part of SE tax claimed, and where is it figured?
notes.back: On Schedule 1, line 15; the amount comes from Schedule SE, line 13.
notes.explanation: It is an adjustment to income, so you don't need to itemize.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1040 and 1040-SR (2025), “Line 15 Deductible Part of Self-Employment Tax”, p. 93
notes.evidence: If you were self-employed and owe self-employment tax, fill in Schedule SE to figure the amount of your deduction. The deductible part of your self-employment tax is on line 13 of Schedule SE.

notes.front: A sole proprietor owes $9,000 of SE tax for 2025. What adjustment to income can she take?
notes.back: $4,500 on Schedule 1, line 15.
notes.explanation: One-half of $9,000 = $4,500 is deductible.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “Self-employment tax”, p. 102
notes.evidence: Deduct one-half of your self-employment tax on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 15.

notes.front: For 2025, the IRA contribution limit is {{c1::$7,000}}.
notes.explanation: The limit stayed the same as for 2024; age 50 or older adds $1,000.
notes.source: Publication 590-A (2025), Contributions to Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “What's New for 2025”, p. 1
notes.evidence: 2025, the IRA contribution limit remains $7,000 ($8,000 for individuals age 50 or older).

notes.front: For 2025, someone aged 50 or older can contribute up to {{c1::$8,000}} to IRAs.
notes.explanation: That is $7,000 plus a $1,000 catch-up for those 50 or older.
notes.source: Publication 590-A (2025), Contributions to Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “What's New for 2025”, p. 1
notes.evidence: 2025, the IRA contribution limit remains $7,000 ($8,000 for individuals age 50 or older).

notes.front: Joy is 52 with $50,000 of wages in 2025. What is the most she can contribute to her IRAs for 2025?
notes.explanation: She is 50 or older, and her compensation exceeds $8,000, so the $8,000 limit applies.
notes.source: Publication 590-A (2025), Contributions to Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “What's New for 2025”, p. 1
notes.evidence: ($8,000 for individuals age 50 or older).

notes.front: A study guide says the IRA limit is $7,500. For which year is that right, and what applies to tax year 2025?
notes.back: $7,500 is the 2026 limit; tax year 2025 uses $7,000 ($8,000 at 50 or older).
notes.explanation: Publication 590-A lists the 2026 increase separately from the 2025 limits.
notes.source: Publication 590-A (2025), Contributions to Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “What's New for 2026”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Beginning in 2026, the IRA contribution limit is increased to $7,500 ($8,600 for individuals age 50 or older) from $7,000 ($8,000 for individuals age 50 or older).

notes.front: For 2025, over what MAGI range is the traditional IRA deduction phased out for a married couple filing jointly, when covered by a plan at work?
notes.back: More than $126,000 but less than $146,000.
notes.explanation: At $146,000 or more there is no deduction.
notes.source: Publication 590-A (2025), Contributions to Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “What's New for 2025”, p. 2
notes.evidence: More than $126,000 but less than $146,000 for a married couple filing a joint return or a qualifying surviving spouse

notes.front: For 2025, over what MAGI range is the traditional IRA deduction phased out for a single filer covered by a plan at work?
notes.back: More than $79,000 but less than $89,000.
notes.explanation: The same range applies to head of household filers.
notes.source: Publication 590-A (2025), Contributions to Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “What's New for 2025”, p. 2
notes.evidence: More than $79,000 but less than $89,000 for a single individual or head of household

notes.front: For 2025, if only your spouse is covered by a plan at work and you file jointly, over what MAGI range is your IRA deduction phased out?
notes.back: More than $236,000 but less than $246,000.
notes.explanation: At $246,000 or more you can't deduct traditional IRA contributions.
notes.source: Publication 590-A (2025), Contributions to Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “What's New for 2025”, p. 2
notes.evidence: phased out if your modified AGI is more than $236,000 (up from $230,000 for 2024) but less than $246,000

notes.front: A married couple filing jointly, both covered by plans at work, have 2025 MAGI of $150,000. Can they deduct traditional IRA contributions?
notes.back: No. Their MAGI is above the $146,000 end of the phase-out.
notes.explanation: $150,000 ≥ $146,000 means no deduction; they can still make nondeductible contributions.
notes.source: Publication 590-A (2025), Contributions to Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Table 1-2”, p. 14
notes.evidence: $146,000 or more no deduction.

notes.front: A single filer covered by a 401(k) has 2025 MAGI of $84,000. Is the IRA deduction full, partial or nil?
notes.back: Partial.
notes.explanation: $84,000 is more than $79,000 but less than $89,000, inside the phase-out range.
notes.source: Publication 590-A (2025), Contributions to Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Table 1-2”, p. 14
notes.evidence: more than $79,000 but less than $89,000 a partial deduction.

notes.front: Under the Kay Bailey Hutchison Spousal IRA limit, what is the most a lower-earning spouse filing jointly can contribute for 2025?
notes.back: The smaller of $7,000 ($8,000 if 50 or older) or the couple's combined compensation less the other spouse's IRA contributions.
notes.explanation: This lets a spouse with little or no pay contribute on the couple's joint compensation.
notes.source: Publication 590-A (2025), Contributions to Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Kay Bailey Hutchison Spousal IRA Limit”, p. 10
notes.evidence: if you file a joint return and your taxable compensation is less than that of your spouse, the most that can be contributed for the year to your IRA is the smaller of the following two amounts.

notes.front: Kris (age 40) had no pay in 2025; spouse Lane (age 45) earned $60,000 and put $7,000 in a traditional IRA. They file jointly. How much can Kris contribute?
notes.explanation: Combined compensation $60,000 − Lane's $7,000 = $53,000. The smaller of $7,000 and $53,000 is $7,000.
notes.source: Publication 590-A (2025), Contributions to Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Kay Bailey Hutchison Spousal IRA Limit”, p. 10
notes.evidence: The total compensation includible in the gross income of both you and your spouse for the year, reduced by the following two amounts.

notes.front: What is the 2025 general limit on elective deferrals to a 401(k)?
notes.explanation: The same limit applies to most section 457 plans.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “What's New”, p. 1
notes.evidence: the total annual amount you can contribute is increased to: • $23,500,

notes.front: Hana is 55 at the end of 2025. What is the most she can defer into her 401(k)?
notes.explanation: Age 50 or older (but not 60–63) raises the limit from $23,500 to $31,000.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What's New”, p. 3
notes.evidence: $31,000 if age 50 or older

notes.front: Ike is 61 at the end of 2025 and in a 401(k). What is his elective deferral limit?
notes.explanation: Ages 60, 61, 62 and 63 at year end get a higher catch-up of $11,250 instead of $7,500: $23,500 + $11,250 = $34,750.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “What's New”, p. 1
notes.evidence: $34,750 if age 60 through 63 at the end of 2025.

notes.front: Jo is 64 at the end of 2025. Which elective deferral limit applies?
notes.back: $31,000, the age-50-or-older limit.
notes.explanation: The higher $34,750 limit covers only ages 60 to 63 at year end; at 64 the age-50-or-older limit of $31,000 applies again.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “What's New”, p. 1
notes.evidence: $31,000 if age 50 or older, or • $34,750 if age 60 through 63 at the end of 2025.

notes.front: If you defer more than the limit, what generally happens to the excess?
notes.back: It must generally be included in your income for that year, unless it is a designated Roth contribution.
notes.explanation: You, not only your employer, are responsible for monitoring your total deferrals.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “Excess deferrals”, p. 53
notes.evidence: If you set aside more than the limit, the excess must generally be included in your income for that year, unless you have an excess deferral of a designated Roth contribution.

notes.front: For 2025, with self-only HDHP coverage, you can contribute up to {{c1::$4,300}} to an HSA.
notes.explanation: Family coverage allows up to $8,550.
notes.source: Publication 969 (2025), Health Savings Accounts and Other Tax-Favored Health Plans, “Limit on Contributions”, p. 5
notes.evidence: For 2025, if you have self-only HDHP coverage, you can contribute up to $4,300.

notes.front: For 2025, with family HDHP coverage, you can contribute up to {{c1::$8,550}} to an HSA.
notes.explanation: Self-only coverage allows up to $4,300.
notes.source: Publication 969 (2025), Health Savings Accounts and Other Tax-Favored Health Plans, “Limit on Contributions”, p. 5
notes.evidence: If you have family HDHP coverage, you can contribute up to $8,550.

notes.front: How much extra can an eligible individual aged 55 or older contribute to an HSA?
notes.explanation: With self-only coverage that makes $4,300 + $1,000 = $5,300.
notes.source: Publication 969 (2025), Health Savings Accounts and Other Tax-Favored Health Plans, “Additional contribution”, p. 6
notes.evidence: If you are an eligible individual who is age 55 or older at the end of your tax year, your contribution limit is increased by $1,000.

notes.front: Gus, 58, has self-only HDHP coverage all of 2025 and no employer contributions. What is his HSA limit?
notes.explanation: $4,300 self-only limit + $1,000 additional contribution at 55 or older = $5,300.
notes.source: Publication 969 (2025), Health Savings Accounts and Other Tax-Favored Health Plans, “Additional contribution”, p. 6
notes.evidence: if you have self-only coverage, you can contribute up to $5,300 (the contribution limit for self-only coverage ($4,300) plus the additional contribution of $1,000).

notes.front: If either spouse has family HDHP coverage, how are both spouses treated?
notes.back: As both having family HDHP coverage.
notes.explanation: The family limit is then split equally unless they agree otherwise.
notes.source: Publication 969 (2025), Health Savings Accounts and Other Tax-Favored Health Plans, “Rules for married people”, p. 6
notes.evidence: If either spouse has family HDHP coverage, both spouses are treated as having family HDHP coverage.

notes.front: Spouses under 55 each have family HDHP coverage under separate plans and no Archer medical savings account. How is the 2025 HSA limit shared if they make no agreement?
notes.back: $8,550 split equally: $4,275 each.
notes.explanation: Their combined limit is $8,550, divided equally absent agreement: $8,550 ÷ 2 = $4,275.
notes.source: Publication 969 (2025), Health Savings Accounts and Other Tax-Favored Health Plans, “Rules for married people”, p. 6
notes.evidence: After that reduction, the contribution limit is split equally between the spouses unless you agree on a different division.

notes.front: How do excludable employer HSA contributions affect your own contribution limit?
notes.back: They reduce what you or anyone else can contribute by the same amount.
notes.explanation: The annual limit covers all contributions together.
notes.source: Publication 969 (2025), Health Savings Accounts and Other Tax-Favored Health Plans, “Employer contributions”, p. 6
notes.evidence: You must reduce the amount you or any other person can contribute to your HSA by the amount of any contributions made by your employer that are excludable from your income.

notes.front: Flo, 40, has self-only HDHP coverage all year; her employer puts $1,000 in her HSA. How much more can she contribute herself for 2025?
notes.explanation: $4,300 limit − $1,000 employer contribution = $3,300.
notes.source: Publication 969 (2025), Health Savings Accounts and Other Tax-Favored Health Plans, “Employer contributions”, p. 6
notes.evidence: You must reduce the amount you or any other person can contribute to your HSA by the amount of any contributions made by your employer that are excludable from your income.

notes.front: Are employer HSA contributions included in the employee's income?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: Contributions by others, such as the employee, are deductible instead.
notes.source: Publication 969 (2025), Health Savings Accounts and Other Tax-Favored Health Plans, “Introduction”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Contributions, other than employer contributions, are deductible on the eligible individual's return whether or not the individual itemizes deductions. Employer contributions aren't included in income.

notes.front: Must you itemize to deduct your own HSA contributions?
notes.back: No. They are deductible whether or not you itemize.
notes.explanation: Publication 969 states the deduction is available without itemizing on Schedule A.
notes.source: Publication 969 (2025), Health Savings Accounts and Other Tax-Favored Health Plans, “Benefits of an HSA”, p. 3
notes.evidence: You can claim a tax deduction for contributions you or someone other than your employer make to your HSA even if you don't itemize your deductions on Schedule A (Form 1040).

notes.front: Gia, an eligible individual, puts $3,000 of her own money into her HSA in 2025 and takes the standard deduction. Can she deduct the $3,000?
notes.back: Yes. Her own HSA contributions are deductible without itemizing.
notes.explanation: Contributions by anyone other than the employer are deductible whether or not you itemize on Schedule A.
notes.source: Publication 969 (2025), Health Savings Accounts and Other Tax-Favored Health Plans, “Benefits of an HSA”, p. 3
notes.evidence: You can claim a tax deduction for contributions you or someone other than your employer make to your HSA even if you don't itemize your deductions on Schedule A (Form 1040).

notes.front: Ned enrolled in Medicare in 2025 but kept his HDHP. Is he an eligible individual for HSA contributions after enrolling?
notes.back: No. Enrollment in Medicare ends eligibility.
notes.explanation: Not being enrolled in Medicare is one of the eligibility requirements.
notes.source: Publication 969 (2025), Health Savings Accounts and Other Tax-Favored Health Plans, “Qualifying for an HSA Contribution”, p. 3
notes.evidence: You aren't enrolled in Medicare.

notes.front: A 22-year-old on an HDHP is claimed as a dependent on a parent's 2025 return. Can he contribute to an HSA?
notes.back: No. Someone who can be claimed as a dependent is not an eligible individual.
notes.explanation: Not being claimable as a dependent is one of the requirements.
notes.source: Publication 969 (2025), Health Savings Accounts and Other Tax-Favored Health Plans, “Qualifying for an HSA Contribution”, p. 3
notes.evidence: You can't be claimed as a dependent on someone else's 2025 tax return.

notes.front: What are the 2025 minimum annual deductibles for an HDHP?
notes.back: $1,650 self-only; $3,300 family.
notes.explanation: The maximum out-of-pocket amounts are $8,300 and $16,600.
notes.source: Publication 969 (2025), Health Savings Accounts and Other Tax-Favored Health Plans, “High deductible health plan (HDHP)”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Minimum annual deductible $1,650 $3,300

notes.front: Ora, 45, first got self-only HDHP coverage on 1 October 2025 and still had it on 1 December. Under the last-month rule, how much can she contribute for 2025?
notes.explanation: Eligible on 1 December, she is treated as eligible all year, so the full $4,300 applies, subject to the testing period.
notes.source: Publication 969 (2025), Health Savings Accounts and Other Tax-Favored Health Plans, “Last-month rule”, p. 3
notes.evidence: you are considered to be an eligible individual for the entire year if you are an eligible individual on the first day of the last month of your tax year

notes.front: Are HSA distributions used for qualified medical expenses taxed?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: Only amounts used exclusively for qualified medical expenses are tax free.
notes.source: Publication 969 (2025), Health Savings Accounts and Other Tax-Favored Health Plans, “Introduction”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Distributions from an HSA that are used to pay qualified medical expenses aren't taxed.

notes.front: Cy withdraws $2,000 from his HSA to pay a hospital bill for qualified medical care. How much is taxable?
notes.back: None.
notes.explanation: Distributions used to pay qualified medical expenses aren't taxed.
notes.source: Publication 969 (2025), Health Savings Accounts and Other Tax-Favored Health Plans, “Introduction”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Distributions from an HSA that are used to pay qualified medical expenses aren't taxed.

notes.front: How is an HSA distribution not used for qualified medical expenses taxed?
notes.back: It is subject to income tax and may be subject to an additional 20% tax.
notes.explanation: Exceptions to the 20% tax apply after disability, age 65 or death.
notes.source: Publication 969 (2025), Health Savings Accounts and Other Tax-Favored Health Plans, “Distributions From an HSA”, p. 8
notes.evidence: If you receive distributions for other reasons, the amount you withdraw will be subject to income tax and may be subject to an additional 20% tax.

notes.front: After which events is there no additional 20% tax on nonmedical HSA distributions?
notes.back: After you become disabled, reach age 65, or die.
notes.explanation: The distribution is still subject to income tax.
notes.source: Publication 969 (2025), Health Savings Accounts and Other Tax-Favored Health Plans, “Additional tax: Exceptions”, p. 10
notes.evidence: There is no additional tax on distributions made after the date you are disabled, reach age 65, or die.

notes.front: Dee, 40 and not disabled, takes $1,000 from her HSA for a holiday. What tax applies?
notes.back: Income tax on $1,000 plus a $200 additional tax.
notes.explanation: Nonmedical use makes it taxable, and 20% × $1,000 = $200 applies since no exception fits.
notes.source: Publication 969 (2025), Health Savings Accounts and Other Tax-Favored Health Plans, “Distributions From an HSA”, p. 8
notes.evidence: the amount you withdraw will be subject to income tax and may be subject to an additional 20% tax.

notes.front: What is the most student loan interest you can deduct for 2025?
notes.back: The smaller of $2,500 or the interest paid in the year.
notes.explanation: The deduction is then subject to a MAGI phase-out.
notes.source: Publication 970 (2025), Tax Benefits for Education, “Figuring the Deduction”, p. 33
notes.evidence: loan interest deduction is generally the smaller of: • $2,500, or • The interest you paid during the tax year.

notes.front: What counts as student loan interest?
notes.back: Interest paid during the year on a qualified student loan, both required and voluntary payments.
notes.explanation: A qualified student loan is one taken out solely to pay qualified education expenses.
notes.source: Publication 970 (2025), Tax Benefits for Education, “Student Loan Interest Defined”, p. 30
notes.evidence: Student loan interest is interest you paid during the year on a qualified student loan. It includes both required and voluntary interest payments.

notes.front: Can a loan from a related person be a qualified student loan?
notes.back: No. It can't be from a related person or made under a qualified employer plan.
notes.explanation: Publication 970's summary table states this loan requirement.
notes.source: Publication 970 (2025), Tax Benefits for Education, “Table 4-1”, p. 30
notes.evidence: Can't be from a related person or made under a qualified employer plan.

notes.front: For 2025, over what MAGI range is the student loan interest deduction phased out?
notes.explanation: At $100,000 ($200,000 joint) or more, no deduction is allowed.
notes.source: Publication 970 (2025), Tax Benefits for Education, “Modified adjusted gross income (MAGI)”, p. 34
notes.evidence: You can't claim a student loan interest deduction if your MAGI is $100,000 or more ($200,000 or more if you file a joint return).

notes.front: Single filer Ula paid $3,100 of qualified student loan interest in 2025 and has MAGI of $60,000. What can she deduct?
notes.explanation: Her MAGI is below $85,000, so no phase-out; the smaller of $2,500 and $3,100 is $2,500.
notes.source: Publication 970 (2025), Tax Benefits for Education, “Figuring the Deduction”, p. 33
notes.evidence: loan interest deduction is generally the smaller of: • $2,500, or • The interest you paid during the tax year.

notes.front: A single filer with 2025 MAGI of $102,000 paid $1,800 of student loan interest. What is the deduction?
notes.back: Nothing.
notes.explanation: MAGI of $100,000 or more eliminates the deduction for a single filer.
notes.source: Publication 970 (2025), Tax Benefits for Education, “Modified adjusted gross income (MAGI)”, p. 34
notes.evidence: You can't claim a student loan interest deduction if your MAGI is $100,000 or more

notes.front: Can a married person filing separately claim the student loan interest deduction?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: Publication 970 allows the student loan interest deduction under any filing status except married filing separately.
notes.source: Publication 970 (2025), Tax Benefits for Education, “Can You Claim the Deduction?”, p. 33
notes.evidence: Your filing status is any filing status except married filing separately.

notes.front: For Armed Forces moving expenses, what is a permanent change of station? Name the moves it includes.
notes.back: A move to your first post of active duty; from one permanent post to another; or from your last post to home or nearer.
notes.explanation: The last kind must occur within 1 year of ending active duty or within the period allowed.
notes.source: Publication 3 (2025), Armed Forces' Tax Guide, “What constitutes a permanent change of station?”, p. 12
notes.evidence: A move from your home to your first post of active duty, • A move from one permanent post of duty to another, and • A move from your last post of duty to your home
